# Scale-up and techno-economic analysis of microbial electrolysis cells for hydrogen production from wastewater

Jinyue Jiang a,b, Juan A. Lopez-Ruiz c, Yanhong Bian a,b, Dongya Sun a,b, Yuqing Yan a,b, Xi Chen a,b, Junjie Zhu a,b, Harold D. May b, Zhiyong Jason Ren a,b,*

Keywords: Microbial electrolysis cell Scale up Techno-economic analysis Microbial electrochemical system Wastewater Hydrogen

A B S T R A C T

Microbial electrolysis cells (MECs) have demonstrated high-rate H2 production while concurrently treating wastewater, but the transition in scale from laboratory research to systems that can be practically applied has encountered challenges. It has been more than a decade since the first pilot-scale MEC was reported, and in recent years, many attempts have been made to overcome the barriers and move the technology to the market. This study provided a detailed analysis of MEC scale-up efforts and summarized the key factors that should be considered to further develop the technology. We compared the major scale-up configurations and systematically evaluated their performance from both technical and economic perspectives. We characterized how system scaleup impacts the key performance metrics such as volumetric current density and H2 production rate, and we proposed methods to evaluate and optimize system design and fabrication. In addition, preliminary technoeconomic analysis indicates that MECs can be profitable in many different market scenarios with or without subsidies. We also provide perspectives on future development needed to transition MEC technology to the marketplace.

## 1. Introduction

The increasing demand for clean energy and water is driving the development of new processes and technologies that provide agile and multifaceted solutions. Microbial electrolysis cells (MECs) are a type of microbial electrochemical system that carry unique functions that accomplish concurrent H2 production and organic waste degradation (Logan et al., 2008; Wang and Ren, 2013). Compared to abiotic elec­ trolysis, MEC technology consumes low to zero energy, and it uses wastewater rather than clean water to produce clean H2 (Jack et al., 2021; Rousseau et al., 2020a). MEC reactors have been tested with a vast range of wastewater streams, including domestic wastewater (Escapa et al., 2012a; Heidrich et al., 2014), animal waste slurry (Cerrillo et al., 2016; Wagner et al., 2009), and a variety of industrial streams from food and beverage, oil and gas, biorefineries, and fermentation effluents (Chen et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2022; Sharma et al., 2014). Results from laboratory to pilot scales have demonstrated the potential for MEC technology to be integrated processes to transform wastewater

treatment into an energy neutral or positive process that yields both economic and environmental benefits (Osset-´Alvarez et al., 2019). A typical MEC reactor involves five major components: (1) an anode, (2) a cathode, (3) an electrolyte, (4) a separator/membrane, and 5) a power source. In an MEC, electroactive microorganisms oxidize sub­ strates from the anolyte and transfer electrons (e−) to the anode as the electron acceptor through direct contact or mediated processes (Logan et al., 2019). The electrons are then used at the cathode to reduce H2O or H+ to H2. The whole-cell reaction for MEC using acetate as substrate can thus be written as:

This difference in EO cell highlights the much lower voltage needed in MEC to drive H2 evolution compared to abiotic water electrolysis. The theoretical energy requirement for MEC is as low as 3.3 kWh⋅kg−1 H2 (0.29 kWh⋅m−3 H2) (Logan et al., 2008), which is more than 90% less than the 39 kWh⋅kg−1 H2 needed for water electrolysis (Ivy, 2004). In addition, because the MEC anode does not produce O2, traditional ion exchange membranes can be omitted to save cost and prevent fouling. Such single-chamber configuration however does generate different sets of challenges such as reduced H2 purity due to CO2 generation from the anode, as well as H2 consumption due to methanogenesis (Call and Logan, 2008; Guo et al., 2010; Hu et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2009). Many studies have reported on advances in MEC development, but most of the studies are still at the laboratory scale with the volume rarely exceeding 1 L. The first scale-up trial of MEC was published in 2011 with a 1000 L reactor (Cusick et al., 2011), after which dozens of pilot studies demonstrated system performance at different reactor configurations, scales, and operational modes. A recent review benchmarked the per­ formance of pilot scale MECs against standard activated sludge pro­ duced during wastewater treatment reported that MECs can treat actual wastewater to effluent standards at a lower energetic cost, but the volumetric treatment rate and reactor depth are the main limiting fac­ tors that prevent commercial application (Leicester et al., 2020a).

Similarly, multiple reviews have summarized the substrates, materials, and reactor performance of pilot-scale studies (Escapa et al., 2016; Kadier et al., 2016; Rousseau et al., 2020a), but the pathway towards scale-up and cost feasibility remains unclear. Therefore, we focused this analytical review on breaking down the mainstream MEC scale-up strategies employed to date. Our review revealed the major technolog­ ical barriers to large system manufacturing and operation. In addition, we evaluated the profitability of MECs under different cost scenarios using techno-economic analysis (TEA) and discussed perspectives on how to finally push this technology to the marketplace. We focused on the studies with total operational volumes larger than 1 L, and for each entry, we summarized available information regarding reactor design, operation conditions, and performance metrics (See Supplementary Table).

## 2. The pilot MEC design schemes

Many groups have reported their pilot MEC configurations, but they can be divided into two major categories: reactor-based or electrodebased modularization (Fig. 1). The concept of reactor modularization was realized by hydraulically connecting several reactor units in series or in parallel to achieve a higher overall volume. When connected in series, the hydraulic retention time was maximized, which could lead to better organic removal, but the treatment capacity was limited. When connected in parallel, treatment capacity and overall H2 production could be increased, but the wastewater treatment efficiency may be limited. Therefore, there is no single optimal configuration, and the selection of configurations should depend on the priority of the design and operation. It is worth noting that the terms “in series” and “in parallel” used here are indications of hydraulic connection and should not be confused with electrical circuit connection. One could easily envision a case in which several reactors run in parallel (side-by-side) but are powered in series by one single power source. Rectangular reactors and tubular reactors are two popular MEC configurations. Widely used rectangular reactors are similar to classic frame-in-plate electrolyzer cells. ## 3. The pilot MEC performance metrics

3.1. Would reactor size and modularization approach make a difference?

Pilot MECs have been actively researched and tested, but their per­ formance inevitably varied significantly. To examine if reactor size was a determining factor, we used key performance metrics including COD removal efficiency, current density, and H2 production rate to evaluate

the effects. Fig. 4B and 4C depict the reactor performance measured by these parameters in relation to reactor unit volume. The unit volume (L) is determined as follows. For MECs with electrode modules or MECs without any modularization, the unit volume is simply their total vol­ ume reported. For MECs with reactor modules, the unit volume is the volume of each reactor module. As shown in Fig. 4B, the COD removal efficiency does not exhibit a clear trend with respect to unit volume, but most studies did demonstrate decent COD removal regardless of the size of the system. The highest achieved COD removal efficiency was 92% in one of the parallel units reported by Escapa et al. (2015) using the pri­ mary effluent from a wastewater treatment plant. In another study in which total organic carbon was reported, nearly 100% removal was observed when primary treatment effluent was treated, although the removal efficiency decreased when sludge centrate was added to the influent (Isabel San-Martín et al., 2018). Among those studies that re­ ported final effluent quality, only a few met a discharge standard of less than 120 mg⋅L−1 COD, and most of these systems were fed with low-strength wastewater (COD <800 mg⋅L−1) (Escapa et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2022; Leicester et al., 2020a). It has been well documented in MEC reactors that the current density drops at low COD values, resulting in slow removal kinetics for the remaining COD (Zhang et al., 2015); hence, MEC alone may not be suitable for meeting discharge limits, rather a coupled process with membrane reactors or electrolyzers may be needed to achieve that goal (Akhade et al., 2020; Lopez-Ruiz et al., 2021; Ren et al., 2014). In contrast to COD, the volumetric current density and the H2 pro­ duction rate in MECs showed a clear reverse trend with respect to the unit volume (Fig. 4C). 3.2. The current density barrier and how to overcome it in pilot reactors

The volumetric H2 production rate reporting liters of H2 produced per liter of reactor per day (L⋅LR −1⋅day−1) has long been used as an important performance metric since the early days of MECs (Call and Logan, 2008; Cheng and Logan, 2007). The use of volumetric rate fol­ lows the tradition in wastewater treatment as MECs were not only used for H2 production but also as a wastewater treatment technology. Such volumetric-based H2 rate is different from the common electrode surface area-based current density (A⋅m−2 or mA⋅cm−2), as traditional water electrolysis does not consider water treatment as a function. The elec­ trolysis community often views that MECs have limited applications as they operate at very low surface area-based current density. However, one should note the cathode reaction in MECs is the same as abiotic electrolysis as the microbial anode reaction is generally the limiting factor. In large-scale applications, anodes with much larger surface areas per unit of cross-sectional area are feasible and, as such will enable much faster wastewater organic removal as well as higher overall current and resulting higher cathode surface area-based current density. Laboratory-scale reactors have achieved higher current densities with more than 10 studies reporting over 10 A⋅m−2, but the majority of pilot-scale MECs only have a current density around or below 1 A⋅m−2. The highest volumetric current density achieved by Singh et al., al. (2021) in a 10 L up-flow MEC (970 A⋅m−3) was four orders of magnitude higher than the lowest (0.07 A⋅m−3), and the high value was partially accomplished by a combination of a compact electrode configuration (S/V ratio of 28.2 m2⋅m−3) and high current density (34.4 A⋅m−2). There are a variety of reasons for the discrepancy between laboratory-scale and pilot-scale reactor performance, even if the con­ figurations are similar. Laboratory-scale reactors often have more ideal flow profiles and architecture, whereas larger reactors possess hydraulic dead zones, electrode blockage, and are more prone to leakage. In addition, the internal resistance of large reactors remains high due to the relatively low conductivity of wastewater as well as increased ohmic resistance of large carbon electrodes (Heidrich et al., 2014). Larger electrode spacings and loose connections are more likely to occur in large reactors as well (Guo et al., 2017; Rousseau et al., 2020b). One important factor that has largely been omitted was the heterogeneity induced by large reactors. Hydrostatic pressure, solid deposition, and dissolved O2 concentrations could be exacerbated in large systems, creating vastly different micro-environments throughout the reactor. For example, San-Martín et al. (2019b) reported vertical stratification of anode microbial communities in two 16 L MECs, with distinct variation at the family taxonomic level observed across electrode sampling points. In laboratory-scale reactors, it is generally assumed that electrostatic potential would be homogeneous along the electrode surface as well as in the bulk electrolyte, but those conditions may not hold true for larger-scale systems. Potential differences along the electrode surface can be compensated using metal current collectors, which is currently adopted by many pilot-scale studies (Carmona-Martínez et al., 2015;

Escapa et al., 2015; Heidrich et al., 2014). This method, however, cannot compensate for the electrostatic potential difference in the bulk elec­ trolyte. For example, numerical modeling revealed that a potential dif­ ference over 50 mV can arise from electrolyte in contact with a 50 cm2

anode (Oliot et al., 2017). This difference is likely to be higher for an­ odes in pilot-scale MECs, where the surface area could be approaching 1 m2. As a result, such a heterogeneous electrode potential could lead to unfavorable growth of non-electroactive microorganisms and high electrical potential loss (Torres et al., 2009).

## 4. The techno-economic analysis of MEC

Analyzing the techno-economic feasibility of an emerging technol­ ogy brings insights on market opportunities and challenges, but to date, limited information is available regarding the economics of MECs (Aiken et al., 2019; Escapa et al., 2016, 2012b; Savla et al., 2021). Here, we performed a preliminary TEA to assess the profitability of MEC based on the revenue from H2 production and the cost from external electricity consumption. The electricity cost was chosen because it is expected to be a substantial part of the operational cost. For instance, electricity was reported to account for almost half of the operational cost in a previous TEA on a MEC-methanol synthesis system (Streeck et al., 2018). It is also the metric that can be most precisely evaluated from existing literature among all cost items. We define profitability in this analysis as the ratio of H2 sale revenue to energy cost (electricity cost). When the profit­ ability ratio is >1, the system earns more revenue from H2 sales than the cost of electricity consumed in the process. Profitability can be calcu­ lated as:

5.2. Sufficient and standard data collection and reporting are needed

Although there are well-established guidelines for reporting MEC results in laboratory-scale studies (Logan et al., 2008), results from pilot studies often vary widely. It is certainly difficult to perform compre­ hensive measurements on all key parameters in large systems, but to advance the technology, coordinated and standard reporting of key parameters would be very valuable. Fig. 8B summarizes 10 common MEC metrics and the number of pilot MEC studies that reported these metrics. The reactor assembly including size, material, and configura­ tion is almost always reported. Current density is also reported for almost all existing pilot literature studies, either normalized by volume or surface area. However, the reporting method is not consistent, as some studies chose to report absolute current expressed in amps or milliamps without normalization, which prohibits a fair comparison across studies (Jadhav et al., 2022a). Though current density can be calculated if volume or surface information were given, unfortunately they are not all provided in the cited studies. Also, some studies only report current or current density but do not report on H2 production data, which is certainly highly desirable. As noted previously, high current density did not necessarily lead to high levels of H2 recovery due to leaking, re-consumption, and other practical challenges. Efficiency metrics, including rcat and coulombic efficiency (CE), are reported in even lower frequency. These two metrics can be useful in­ dicators of MEC system malfunctions as well as side reactions. A CE greater than 100% indicates that an alternate electron donor is present and is contributing to the current. In most cases, a CE >100% indicates H2 recycling; that is, H2 can be directly oxidized either in the anode or is consumed by homoacetogens and converted to acetate or

## 5. What it takes to make MECs market-relevant

5.1. High-strength wastewater would be an ideal entry point

Most pilot MECs used actual wastewater as electrolyte, but as mentioned, the ionic conductivity has been a major hurdle in large-scale reactors. Fig. 8A summarizes the relationship between wastewater ionic conductivity and current density reported by pilot-scale MECs, and it clearly depicts that higher conductivity led to higher current density. Higher conductivity reduces the system internal resistance and facilitates ion transfer, and that is why almost all synthetic electrolytes used buffer solutions (Kadier et al., 2016; Sleutels et al., 2009). Some studies added salts to improve wastewater MEC conductivity, but caution should be taken as non-buffering salts such as NaCl will compete with buffering components in the ion-migration flux and exacerbate local acidification at the bioanode, which causes unfavorable thermodynamics and irreversibly deteriorating bioanode activity (Oliot et al., 2016; Satinover et al., 2020; Torres et al., 2008). Adding buffering salt can alleviate such problems, but the cost can be prohibitive. The highest current densities achieved in pilot-scale MECs so far, including 90 A⋅m− 2

reported by Rousseau et al. (2020b) and 42.3 A⋅m− 2 by Carmona-- Martínez et al. (2015), were both obtained with a high salt electrolyte (i. e., 45 g⋅L− 1 and 35 g⋅L− 1 NaCl addition, respectively) and halotolerant

using actual wastewater is another major challenge to overcome for realworld applications. It has been documented before that long-term operation could lead to performance drop for a variety of reasons (Heidrich et al., 2014). One of the top reasons is the competition from methanogenesis, as methanogens in the electrolyte will grow and oxidize acetate, formate, or H2 as the electron donor for the production of methane. A recent review provided a great summary of the strategies to inhibit methanogenesis, including shortening hydraulic retention time, harvesting H2 out, lowering the temperature, and controlling pH (He et al., 2022). Another cause of reduced performance is the defi­ ciency in micronutrients like minerals that are required for sustaining microbial activity, which can be resolved by periodical supplementa­ tion, though the cost needs to be carefully considered. Other reasons may include influent toxicity, electrode potential deviation, and biofilm deterioration. The constant monitoring of the electrode potential, elec­ troactive biofilm, temperature and pH, and other parameters would be critical to detect and address these problems. For example, monitoring the anode potential could help in deciding the appropriate applied voltage, as a proper range of anode potential is vital to biofilm perfor­ mance. In large-scale operations, it is not uncommon to switch between different modes of power supply. During the inoculation stage, a lower set anode potential helps accelerate electroactive biofilm formation. After that, a higher potential could reduce energy input, facilitate organic degradation, and increase overall current and H2 production (Ren et al., 2011). Beside electrochemical measures, biofilm monitoring using imaging or omics tools could also provide valuable information on the viability and composition of the biofilm and shed light on the longevity of reactor operation. From such a perspective, the reactor design should consider the easy accessibility of the individual electrodes for sampling and monitoring without operation interruption. Beside these direct measurements, a periodic check on rcat and CE is also rec­ ommended as discussed in Section 5.2.

## 6. To H2 and beyond

More than 10 years have passed since the first scale-up of MEC technology. Since then, we have seen increasing interest in bringing MEC closer to industrial application. We have witnessed great progress along the way, although some challenges remain unsolved for pilot studies. The current density needs to be further increased; however, this is limited by the metabolic rate of the microbes. The incorporation of thermophilic strains while increasing the reactor temperature might provide an interesting solution. Thermophiles usually have a higher metabolic rate compared to strains that thrive at room temperature and thus can sustain a higher current density in the microbial electro­ chemical system. Moreover, the incorporation of thermophiles can take advantage of some high-temperature industrial waste streams while probably avoiding methanogens at the same time. It has also been proposed that thermophiles might be able to degrade a broader spec­ trum of organic compounds, including some recalcitrant species that are resistant to microbial degradation at room temperature (Rathinam et al., 2019). Beside thermophilic strains, halophilic bacteria could also play an important role. In Section 5.1, we discussed the importance of con­ ductivity in improving current. Therefore, the use of high-strength wastewaters as electrolytes, along with halophilic bacteria, is worth considering. We have seen an increasing number of studies in which a halophilic biofilm was inoculated from saline environments (Carmo­ na-Martínez et al., 2015; Rousseau et al., 2020b). On the other hand, thermophilic studies remain scarce. Selection by creating a niche that is favorable to the strains wanted has been the primary way for inoculating a bioanode with specific traits so far. Genetic engineering might aid in this process to create microbes that meet the aforementioned criteria. Beside high temperatures, operating MECs under elevated pressure is another strategy worth considering. 5.3. Balance the pros and cons of scale-up configurations

While each MEC reactor scale-up approach has its advantages and challenges, the quantitative analyses provided in this study shed some light on key considerations. Fig. 8C summarizes the strengths and weaknesses of each configuration discussed, and several major considerations are worthy of discussion. First, modularized cathode assembly appears to be effective in obtaining high current levels and preventing H2 leakage and re-consumption, so if its cost can be reduced, such a design can be promising. On the other hand, single-chamber systems would encounter difficulties in actual open wastewater conditions due to methanogenesis and contamination unless those barriers could be overcome. Second, the flow pattern may be an easy parameter to optimize, as hydrodynamic analysis can help improve kinetics, reduce dead zones, and improve conversion efficiency. Such analysis has been carried out in laboratory-scale reactors (Gao et al., 2021, 2020; Hern´andez-García et al., 2020), and can be applied in pilot-scale reactors. Many pilot-scale MEC studies use electrode modules and placed them on alternate sides of the reactor body to act as baffles, thus forming a serpentine flow pattern. This design resembles the disinfection contact tanks and prolongs contact time to improve COD conversion via a plug-flow configuration. The electrode assemblies at the front of the reactor will encounter heavy organic loadings and will generate most of the H2, while modules at the back end of the reactor may suffer from insufficient electron donors. Other considerations worth noting include the difficulty in bioanode inoculation for large reactors. Several studies have mentioned that the inoculation stage took much longer than laboratory-scale reactors, from weeks to several months (Brown et al., 2014; Cusick et al., 2011; Escapa et al., 2015; San-Martín et al., 2019b). Modularizing the electrodes, therefore, would provide a unique advantage in introducing faster inoculation, as the individual electrode modules can be inoculated separately in smaller containers first before transferring them into the large reactors. However, to the best of our knowledge, such a practice has not been tested in pilot-scale studies.

Operating at an elevated pressure can yield pressurized H2 directly from MEC, which saves the energy needed for downstream compression, and the H2 produced can be readily available for use or sale. Most currently available commercial proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers already operate with an outlet pressure of 30–40 bars (Hancke et al., 2022). Operating a MEC process under such pressure would make it more competitive compared to existing technology. However, high-pressure conditions could also give rise to safety concerns and potential leakages, for which experience from the water electrolysis industry could potentially offer valuable insights. Beside experimental research, modeling is also crucial to advancing our understanding of MECs. Past models have provided valuable information regarding the mass transfer (Yan et al., 2021), potential distribution (Lacroix et al., 2014), biofilm kinetics (Kato Marcus et al., 2007; Pinto et al., 2011; Rimboud et al., 2015), and electrode topography (Champigneux et al., 2018). However, there are some aspects that are less modeled but could shed light on future pilot design. For example, hydraulic modeling of pilot-scale MECs can provide guidance on eliminating hydraulic dead zones and improving mass transfer. In recent years, machine learning has evolved as a powerful tool for environmental researchers (Hino et al., 2018; Zhong et al., 2021). We have started to see its application in the MET field as well (Cai et al., 2019; Du et al., 2022; Fang et al., 2013; Lesnik and Liu, 2017). We believe that machine learning could provide exciting insights into pilot-scale MEC designs in the future; however, incorporating machine learning should be done with caution. Most notably, datasets should be sufficient in size to enable the development of a meaningful machine learning model. Other problems such as data leakage and confounding variables should be handled carefully to avoid misleading results (Riley, 2019; Whalen et al., 2022). While the bulk of pilot MEC studies is dedicated to wastewater treatment and H2 recovery, several pilot-scale MECs are built for other functions. For instance, Sim et al.
